task: Our neighbor's 13-year-old golden retriever Biscuit died this morning. I want to write a short handwritten card to go in her mailbox tomorrow, something warm that mentions how Biscuit always waited for the mail carrier.
rewrite:
ambition:     Lead with Biscuit's name and the loss in plain words, then give one specific image (Biscuit waiting for the mail carrier) and what it meant to you. Leave out the usual sympathy-card lines: "at least it was a long life," "rainbow bridge," "let me know if you need anything."
agency:       The raw material is your own memory of those moments: where Biscuit waited (window, porch, gate), roughly when, and what Biscuit did when the carrier came. Only the waiting is given, so the card uses just that and invents no other details.
acceleration: Use the standard bereavement-note shape: name the loss, one true memory, what the pet meant, a short warm close. Keep it to about 50 to 70 words in plain spoken sentences that fit a small card and read naturally in handwriting.
accuracy:     Nothing outside you can check this. The closest proxy is reading it aloud once and confirming that every detail is something you actually saw and that it sounds like you. A line that rings false to you will ring false to your neighbor.

deeper task:
Write a short, warm, handwritten-style sympathy card from me to my neighbor, whose 13-year-old golden retriever Biscuit died this morning. It will go in her mailbox tomorrow. Open with Biscuit's name and the loss, stated plainly. Use one concrete memory: Biscuit always waited for the mail carrier. Say briefly what that image meant to me as a neighbor. Skip silver linings, "rainbow bridge," "lived a long life," and vague offers of help. Keep it to about 50 to 70 words in plain, spoken sentences, so it fits a small card and is easy to write by hand. Don't invent any other details about Biscuit. Leave blanks only for her name and mine.

answers.plain:
I'm sorry about Biscuit. Thirteen years is a long time to have a dog next door. Here's a card you can adapt:

---

Dear [Name],

I was so sorry to hear about Biscuit. Thirteen years is a lifetime of love, and she was a big part of our street.

I'll always remember how she waited for the mail carrier, so faithful and so sure that the day's most important visitor was on the way. It always made me smile.

We'll miss seeing her by the window. Thinking of you and holding you close. If you ever want company or a walk, I'm just next door.

With love,
[Your name]

---

Some tips for the handwritten version:

- **Keep it short.** A handwritten card with three or four sentences is plenty. Cut the second paragraph down if the space is tight.
- **Use a specific memory.** The mail carrier detail is perfect. If you have another small one, like a wagging tail at the fence or a favorite spot, add it in.
- **Offer something concrete,** but only if you mean it. "I'm next door" is easy for them to accept.

If you tell me more about your relationship with your neighbor, I can make the tone warmer or more formal. I can also write a shorter version.
answers.nudge:
Here's a card short enough to handwrite without cramping, with a couple of alternatives.

**Main version**

> Dear [Name],
>
> I was so sorry to hear about Biscuit. Thirteen years is a long time to love a dog, and a long time for her to love you back.
>
> I'll always picture her waiting for the mail carrier, so sure that the best part of her day was about to show up. She made the whole street feel a little more welcome.
>
> We're thinking of you, and there's no need to reply. If you ever want company, a walk, or just someone to talk about her with, our door is open.
>
> With love,
> [Your name]

**Shorter version, if you want less to write**

> Dear [Name],
>
> We were heartbroken to hear about Biscuit. I'll never forget how she waited for the mail carrier every day, tail going, like it was the best moment of her life. Thirteen years of that kind of joy is a gift, and she gave it to all of us on the street.
>
> Thinking of you,
> [Your name]

**More personal version, if you were close**

> Dear [Name],
>
> The street is quieter today. Biscuit waiting for the mail carrier was part of our mornings, and I'm going to miss seeing her there. I can only imagine how much more you miss her.
>
> I'm so sorry. She was a lucky dog to have you, and you were lucky to have her for thirteen years.
>
> I'm here if you need anything at all.
> [Your name]

**What makes a card like this land well**

- **Add one detail only you saw.** The mail carrier detail is the heart of the card. If you have a second small memory, like the spot she lay in or how she greeted you, swap it in. Specific memories mean more than general sympathy.
- **Use her name.** Writing "Biscuit" plainly is a comfort. Avoid "just a dog," "at least she lived a long life," and "she's in a better place." Even kindly meant, they can sound like they're minimizing the loss.
- **Say "no need to reply."** It takes the pressure off, and the offer of a walk or a chat is easy to accept later.
- **Make the offer concrete if you mean it.** "Our door is open" is fine, but "I'm happy to bring dinner Thursday" is easier to say yes to. Only offer what you'll follow through on.
- **Write it in pen on plain, quiet card stock.** A cheerful pattern can feel off. If you have a photo of Biscuit, tuck it in. A photo of her at the mailbox or window would be perfect, if you have one.
- **Keep it to about 60 to 80 words** and write a rough draft first, so the handwriting stays steady and unhurried. Small crossed-out words are fine. They read as sincere.
- **Put the card in the mailbox tomorrow, or hand-deliver it.** If you'd rather not knock, tuck it in the door or mailbox with no stamp. Your timing is good. The first days are when the house feels quietest.

If you tell me her name and one more thing you remember about Biscuit, I can tailor the wording.
